summary: An excerpt from a fiction book (Book 11, part 32) set in the village of Riverboro along Pleasant River. It opens with Abner Simpson's story of being cheated by a red-haired, hare-lipped stranger who swapped a sleigh for an old cider press and took his money, which the sheriff mocks. It then describes the Simpson children and Mrs. Simpson's work, the village gossip that passes time at the bridge, hayfield, and village store, and Delia Weeks, who leaves Riverboro to keep house for her cousin Cyrus in Lewiston and says she was worn down by village gossip about her secrets.
one_line: Excerpt from a fiction book set in Riverboro, where Abner is cheated in a sleigh-and-cider-press swap and village gossip is examined through Delia Weeks.
key_facts: Abner avowed his complete innocence and told neighbors that a red-haired man with a hare lip and a pepper-and-salt suit had offered to swap him a good sleigh for an old cider press.
Abner paid the hare-lipped stranger four dollars and seventy-five cents to boot in the sleigh swap.
The stranger set down the sleigh, took the cider press on his cart, and vanished up the road, never to be seen again.
Abner declared, "If I could once ketch that consarned old thief... I'd make him dance."
The sheriff replied, "You'll never ketch him, Ab," saying nobody had seen the stranger, the cider press, or the four-seventy-five but Abner.
Mrs. Simpson, described as Abner's better half, took in washing and went out to do days' cleaning.
The town helped feed and clothe the Simpson children.
George, a lanky boy of fourteen, did chores on neighboring farms.
The other Simpson children named are Samuel, Clara Belle, Susan, Elijah, and Elisha, who went to school when sufficiently clothed.
The villages along the banks of Pleasant River had no secrets, and life wore away so quietly that there was much time for conversation.
Meeting-places for talk included the hayfield at noon, the bridge at nightfall, and the stove in the village store of an evening.
Choir rehearsals, sewing societies, reading circles, and church picnics gave opportunity for the expression of feminine opinion.
Delia Weeks was a maiden lady who did dressmaking in a small way and fell ill, sinking slowly into a decline.
Delia Weeks went to keep house for her cousin Cyrus in Lewiston, and in a year grew into a robust, hearty, cheerful woman.
Delia Weeks said, "I was bein' worn to a shadder here, tryin' to keep my little secrets to myself, an' never succeedin'."
